title: The Data Marketplace for Agents
summary: Agents can search the public web at a pace no person can match, but the most valuable data is still hard to reach. Orthogonal connects those agents with the companies that collect, structure, and maintain it.
body_markdown:
Google organized the world's public information. Anything on the open web became searchable, and you could find it almost instantly by clicking through pages.


Agents now do that for us at a pace no person can match. They run many searches at once, read hundreds or thousands of websites, and pull together the answer. But all of it is still limited to public information.


## The data agents can't reach


So much of the valuable data isn't on the open web. Companies have done the hard, painful work of finding it, aggregating it, structuring it and keeping it high quality. Some of it is proprietary. Some of it is technically public but very hard to assemble and maintain. Either way, agents have no easy way to reach it today.


Models are trained on most of the public internet. But when an agent needs live information, it has to search the web. When it needs something specific, like niche data, data about a person, or detailed financial, real estate or car data, it hits a wall. That is exactly the data high-value work depends on.


This isn't a new problem. Long before agents, companies wanted this data inside their products. A company building sales tools needed data on people and companies. A financial product needed the latest, highest-quality financial data. Real estate and car products needed the freshest, most accurate, cleanest data they could get.


That need created a whole industry of data and API companies. An API is just an easy way for software to request data. These companies are essentially structuring the web: they collect information, clean it, and keep it current as it changes. Take job postings. New roles go up and old ones come down every day, and that churn is a valuable signal. It can point to sales opportunities, show how healthy a company is, or reveal what a company is prioritizing.


With agents, people are building new products faster than ever, and this kind of data is becoming more valuable. It's the one kind of information agents can't be trained on, because it's highly specific and always changing. That's where we come in. We bridge the gap between these data companies, more of which are being created every year, and the agents that need them.


Agents are becoming the main way people use the internet. They act on our behalf, proactively, and search the web at a pace that makes a search engine feel unnecessary. But agents don't have this proprietary data. We sit in the middle and connect the two in a way that works for both sides.


## Why the old model breaks


The way these companies sell made sense for their old customers. You sign up, buy a subscription or a block of credits, and then use the product. Those customers wanted that one source and made many requests to it. An agent works differently. It needs a little information from many places. It makes no sense for an agent to sign up, enter a card, and track credit balances across dozens of products. If it's doing research that needs financial data, job data and real estate data, why should it buy three subscriptions it will barely use, or make one or two requests to?


## A marketplace built for agents


So we built a marketplace. Companies that provide data or services list their products once. Agents search, access and pay only when they make a request, only for the small piece of information they actually need. Say an agent wants every new apartment listing in New York. That might be a single request, and the company with that data can charge a cent or a fraction of a cent for it, instead of the $20, $30, $40 or $200 subscriptions of the old model.


Agents are already outpacing people on the web, and we believe that gap will keep growing to 10 or even 100 agents for every person. They'll do more complex work and need more information and more services. We give them one place to search by intent, find the provider that best fits the job, and use and pay for that data or service in the moment. That's where we sit, and that's the problem we're solving.


## One connection, many providers


Our customers already use us to reach many data sources. Some use 7 different providers through Orthogonal. Without us, they'd set up a subscription with each one, connect each one to their agents, and decide every month whether each one is still worth paying for.


As developers, we know that pain well. Do we pay for a subscription to something we haven't even tested? Do we want all these different API products wired into our code? Probably not.


What we offer is flexibility, ease of use, easy access, and a simple way to connect your agents to anything they need, so you can get your work done, build the products you want, and reach the data that gives your workflow an edge. By removing that friction, we give you your time back to focus on what really matters: your product and your customers.


That's what we're doing at Orthogonal. We're building a marketplace for people who want to do more, and for the companies that did the hard, painful work and want to reach the people who value it.
